performers: Magda Tagliaferro, piano; Orchestre des Concerts Lamoureux; Jean Fournet
intro: Saint-Saëns called this slow movement a voyage to the Orient: a Nubian love song in G, a chirruping episode in F♯ major, a cadenza like a Spanish guitar. Magda Tagliaferro plays it with Jean Fournet and the Lamoureux orchestra in Paris, 1954.

sections.label: A · Syncopated chords, then piano runs
B · The Nubian love song in G
C · The F♯ episode: chirruping and tam-tam
sections.mNote: Soft chirruping and tam-tam under a pentatonic melody

sections.label: A′ · Opening material returns, then silence
sections.mNote: Opening material recalled; the music fades out

cues.title: A chord, then runs
cues.text: The orchestra opens with a sharp chord and syncopated string rhythms. The piano answers with runs and an Arabic-sounding theme: the first stop in what Saint-Saëns called a voyage to the Orient.
cues.evidence: The Utah Symphony | Utah Opera listening guide describes the movement opening with a percussive bang and a peppery announcement in the strings. https://usuo.org/explore/2016/03/saint-saens-piano-concerto-no-5-egyptian/ Hannah Chan-Hartley’s programme note for the National Arts Centre (Canada) describes energetic orchestral syncopations and the piano’s Arabic-sounding theme. https://nac-cna.ca/en/event/notes/38409 The composer’s “voyage to the Orient” is quoted in Peter Jost’s preface to Henle HN 1144 (as cited from Dandelot). https://www.henle.de/Piano-Concerto-no.-5-F-major-op.-103-Egyptian/HN-1144
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Thirty-five pages in four days
cues.text: Saint-Saëns writes the concerto at speed. He reaches Cairo on Sunday 22 March 1896, rushes to his manuscript paper the next day, and reports 35 pages of score by 26 March. He tells his publisher on 16 April that it was finished the day before.
cues.evidence: Peter Jost’s preface to the Henle Urtext edition (HN 1144, Munich, spring 2018) quotes Saint-Saëns’s letters to Durand of 26 March 1896 (arrived Sunday 22nd, 35 pages by then) and 16 April 1896 (“finished yesterday”), citing Sabina Teller Ratner’s thematic catalogue. https://www.henle.de/Piano-Concerto-no.-5-F-major-op.-103-Egyptian/HN-1144

cues.title: A love song from the Nile
cues.text: The piano brings in a tender melody in G. Saint-Saëns said it was a Nubian love song he heard boatmen sing on the Nile. Piano and orchestra then take it up together.
cues.evidence: Saint-Saëns’s remark that “the passage in G is a Nubian love song that I heard sung by boatmen on the Nile” is quoted in Peter Jost’s preface to Henle HN 1144. https://www.henle.de/Piano-Concerto-no.-5-F-major-op.-103-Egyptian/HN-1144 Hannah Chan-Hartley’s programme note has the piano introduce the melody and piano and orchestra elaborate it. https://nac-cna.ca/en/event/notes/38409
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Crickets, frogs and a tam-tam
cues.text: The music slips into a distant F♯ major. Quiet chirruping lies beneath a Chinese-sounding melody, with soft blows on the tam-tam. Saint-Saëns described crickets and frogs, and said the voyage here reaches the Far East.
cues.evidence: Hugh Macdonald’s Boston Symphony Orchestra note describes “a strange chirruping in the distant key of F-sharp major, beneath which a Chinese melody is heard against soft blows on the tam-tam.” https://www.bso.org/works/piano-concerto-no-5-egyptian Phillip Borg-Wheeler’s Hyperion booklet note gives the crickets and frogs as the composer’s own description. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/notes/67331-B.pdf The “episode in F-sharp” that “even reaches the Far East” is quoted in the Henle preface.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A Spanish guitar
cues.text: A cadenza follows that sounds like a Spanish guitar. The movement has at least as much Spanish flavour as Egyptian.
cues.evidence: Hannah Chan-Hartley’s programme note has “a Spanish guitar–like cadenza” after the F♯ episode. https://nac-cna.ca/en/event/notes/38409 Phillip Borg-Wheeler’s Hyperion note finds at least as much Spanish flavour as exotic influence in the movement. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/notes/67331-B.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The opening comes back
cues.text: The opening material returns, and the movement fades out into silence.
cues.evidence: Hannah Chan-Hartley’s programme note: after the cadenza “the opening material is recalled, and the movement fades out hauntingly.” https://nac-cna.ca/en/event/notes/38409
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fifty years after the first concert
cues.text: On 2 June 1896 Saint-Saëns plays the concerto at his jubilee concert in the Salle Pleyel, fifty years after his debut, with the Conservatoire orchestra under Paul Taffanel. Reviewing it in Le Monde musical, Édouard Mangeot says he has never heard a work more colourful or gripping.
cues.evidence: Peter Jost’s preface to Henle HN 1144 gives the jubilee concert at the Salle Pleyel on 2 June 1896 with the Conservatoire orchestra under Paul Taffanel, and quotes Mangeot in Le Monde musical (cited from Dandelot, La Vie et l’Œuvre de Saint-Saëns, 1930, pp. 147 f.) among the reactions to the concerto’s first performances. The preface does not say which performance he heard. https://www.henle.de/Piano-Concerto-no.-5-F-major-op.-103-Egyptian/HN-1144

composer.epithet: A pianist at ten and an organist for twenty years, he wrote the Organ Symphony, a dance of skeletons with a xylophone, and a zoo he forbade anyone to print.
facts: Piano with Stamaty; organ with François Benoist and composition under Halévy at the Paris Conservatoire, from 1848
Organist of La Madeleine, 1857–77; piano professor at the École Niedermeyer, 1861–65; co-founder of the Société nationale de musique, 1871
Symphonies, ten concertos, four symphonic poems, operas, organ music, songs and chamber music; also plays, poems and articles
Spent most winters from 1873 in Algeria, Egypt or the Canary Islands, and kept no fixed address from 1889 to 1905

quote.text: I have given it all that I had to give. What I have done I shall never do again.
quote.source: Saint-Saëns on the Organ Symphony, as quoted in Hugh Macdonald’s Boston Symphony Orchestra note

composer.background:
Camille Saint-Saëns was born at 3 rue du Jardinet in Paris on 9 October 1835. His father, a clerk in the Ministry of the Interior, died of consumption on 30 December, when the boy was not yet three months old. Two widows raised the sickly boy: his mother Clémence and her aunt Charlotte Masson, who taught him piano. At two and a half he pressed the keys one at a time and waited for each note to die away before the next. By his own account he already listened to the kettle on the drawing-room fire, a “microscopic oboe” that swelled until the water boiled.

Children’s pieces gave the left hand nothing to do. “The bass doesn’t sing,” he told his teachers in disgust, and was given Haydn and Mozart. On 6 May 1846, aged ten, he played Beethoven’s Third Piano Concerto and a Mozart concerto in B♭ at the Salle Pleyel, with the whole programme from memory. Someone asked his mother what he would play when he was twenty. “He will play his own,” she said.
